The Primitive Who Wanted to Join the Object Club

Int is a hardworking little number. But the Object Club has one rule: only objects allowed. Follow Int's journey to discover wrapper classes, autoboxing, and unboxing.

THE STORY

The Story of Int and the Object Club

Int's journey to the Object Club

A TALE IN SIX MOMENTS

Meet Int. Follow the problem, the helpful wrapper, and the little bit of Java magic that gets Int through the door.

1 · Rejected2 · Help arrives3 · New identity4 · Auto entry5 · Return trip6 · The family
🚫

Int is turned away

Int can store the value 10, but int is a primitive type—not an object. Some Java features, such as generic collections, expect objects.

“I can store a number… so why can't I get in?”
int x = 10;
🎁

A wrapper offers help

The Integer class wraps the primitive value in an object representation. Other wrappers do the same for other primitive types.

“I'll help you enter the object world!”
Integer obj = Integer.valueOf(10);
🦸

Int gets a new identity

The value is now represented by an Integer object. The value is still 10, but the variable's type is now a wrapper class.

“Same value, new form: I'm an Integer!”
Integer obj = Integer.valueOf(x);
✨

The automatic entrance

Java can create the wrapper object for you when you assign a primitive to its matching wrapper type. This convenience is called autoboxing.

“Java did the wrapping for me!”
Integer obj = 10; // autoboxing
🔓

Int can return home

When a primitive is needed, Java can extract the value from its wrapper object. This automatic reverse conversion is called unboxing.

“Back to a simple int. Easy!”
int x = obj; // unboxing
👨‍👩‍👧‍👦

The whole family arrives

Int isn't the only one. Every primitive type has a corresponding wrapper class. The names are classes, so most start with a capital letter.

“There's a wrapper for everyone!”
int → Integer
char → Character

Meet the wrapper family

Remember the pairs. Java collections use wrapper types such as Integer, not primitive types such as int.

Primitive typeWrapper classExample
byteByteByte b = 10;
shortShortShort s = 10;
intIntegerInteger i = 10;
longLongLong l = 10L;
floatFloatFloat f = 10.5f;
doubleDoubleDouble d = 10.5;
charCharacterCharacter c = 'A';
booleanBooleanBoolean ok = true;

Note: void has the special reference type Void, but it is not a wrapper for a normal primitive value in the same way as these eight pairs.

Try Int's transformation

Change the value and run the example. This small demo illustrates the steps Java performs.

🧪

Wrapper workshop

Primitive → Wrapper object → Primitive

Java code
// Autoboxing
int x = 10;
Integer obj = x;

// Unboxing
int y = obj;
What happens
Primitive x = 10
Wrapper obj = 10
Primitive y = 10

Same value, different type.

In Java, wrapper objects are immutable. Unboxing a null wrapper throws a NullPointerException, so check for null when needed.

The moral of the story

Wrapper classes act as a bridge between primitive values and objects in Java, letting values be used in object-oriented features such as collections and generics. Autoboxing: primitive → wrapper. Unboxing: wrapper → primitive.
